objective: By the end of this lesson you can enter a constant-airspeed climb by instruments alone, hold airspeed and heading in straight and turning climbs, and level off at an assigned altitude within ACS limits.
why: Climbing out of trouble, or climbing on an ATC vector, may have to happen with no horizon. A smooth climb on instruments, with the right instruments in charge, keeps you from overcontrolling into a stall or a spiral.

prereading.what: Straight climbs: entry, primary instruments, leveling off, common errors.
prereading.label: IFH 7-14 to 7-19

prereading.what: Standard-rate turns and turns to headings.
prereading.label: IFH 7-19 to 7-20

prereading.what: The same climb on a glass (PFD) panel.
prereading.label: IFH 7-46 to 7-48

prereading.what: Why a climb needs more power, left-turning tendencies, climbing turns, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 3-19 to 3-20

prereading.what: Inversion illusion and the climbing-while-turning illusion.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-8 to 17-9

warmup: You raise the nose for a climb but don't touch the throttle. What happens to your airspeed, and which instrument tells you first?

key_terms.def: A climb at a set power where you hold one airspeed with pitch. The rate of climb is whatever results [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
A climb where you hold a set VSI rate; the VSI becomes primary for pitch and airspeed primary for power once stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
The power setting the POH/AFM gives for climbing [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Starting the level-off before the target altitude, about 10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
In a nose-high attitude the descending (right) prop blade takes a bigger bite, yawing the nose left [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
An abrupt change from climb to level flight that feels like tumbling backward [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

body.p: For a given power and load there is one attitude that gives the most efficient climb. The POH/AFM gives the airspeed and climb power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Those speeds are for max gross weight, so know how they change with weight [[23:207|IFH 7-46]].

bullets: A climb needs extra lift, which makes extra induced drag. That's why climb needs more power than cruise [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
As you add power, slipstream on the tail can raise the nose more than you want [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
P-factor and torque roll and yaw you left. Hold right rudder and some aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
As speed bleeds off, the nose tends to drop unless you add back pressure. Then trim nose-up [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Normally aspirated engines lose power as you climb, so keep nudging the throttle to hold climb power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

callout.text: In the climb, power is fixed. Pitch controls airspeed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: Attitude plus power equals performance. The same picture on the attitude indicator gives very different results in different airplanes [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]:

In the IFH example, a small airplane at full power with the nose two bar widths up climbs 500 fpm at 90 knots. A jet with the same picture climbs 2,000 fpm at 250 knots [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Learn the pictures for your own airplane.

check.q: In a constant-airspeed climb, what controls airspeed: pitch or power?
check.a: Pitch. Power stays at the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: The primary instruments change as the climb develops [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]:

head: Phase
Primary pitch
Primary bank
Primary power
rows: None labeled; attitude indicator and VSI support

body.p: During entry you raise the miniature airplane on the attitude indicator to the climb picture and set power; the figure labels the power gauge as primary [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Once the climb is steady, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the heading indicator stays primary for bank [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Constant-rate climb: airspeed is primary for pitch until the VSI nears the rate you want. Then the VSI is primary for pitch and airspeed is primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

On a glass panel it's the same idea: raise the yellow chevron to the planned pitch, then add climb power. Once stable, airspeed is primary for pitch, heading for bank, tach or manifold pressure for power [[23:207|IFH 7-46]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

check.q: You're stable in a constant-airspeed climb. Which instrument is primary for pitch?

head: Instrument
What can fool you in a climb
Source
rows: Lags behind a pitch change. A large, abrupt change gives erratic and even reversed readings. Use smooth changes.
Very little instrument lag; the delay you see is the airplane slowing down.
May show slight nose-up in rapid acceleration and nose-down in rapid deceleration.
Affected by climbing, power changes and speed changes; leads and lags in turns.
Drifts; check it against the compass at least every 15 minutes.

body.p: Blockages show up clearly in a climb:

bullets: Static port blocked: the altimeter freezes and the VSI stays at zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Airspeed reads lower than actual as you climb above the altitude where it blocked [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].
Pitot tube and drain hole blocked: the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. In a climb it shows a higher and higher airspeed [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

callout.text: A pitot tube blocked together with its drain hole shows airspeed rising in a climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. If you pitch up to "fix" it, the real airspeed drops. Cross-check the attitude indicator and power before believing one instrument [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: You're climbing but the airspeed keeps going up and the attitude and power haven't changed. What might be wrong?
check.a: A blocked pitot tube and drain hole; the airspeed indicator is acting like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

body.p: Entry from cruise, straight ahead [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]:

bullets: 1. Raise the miniature airplane to the nose-high picture for your climb speed, with light back pressure.
2. Add climb power, either with the pitch change or once the speed nears climb speed.
3. Hold right rudder for the left-turning tendency and keep the heading [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
4. Trim off the back pressure as the airplane slows [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
5. Watch the VSI: it should trend up right away, then settle at a steady rate.
6. Once stable, use airspeed as primary for pitch. Airspeed low or high? Make a small pitch correction.

body.p: Entry from climb speed: slow to climb speed in level flight first, then raise the nose and add power at the same time [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Power added after the pitch change lets airspeed drop; power added first makes it rise [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

Climbing turns: combine the straight-climb technique with your turn technique, and speed up your cross-check [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Keep the bank shallow; steep banks cut climb performance a lot [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Standard-rate bank is about 15 percent of true airspeed: about 15° at 100 knots, 18° at 120 knots [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Roll out early by half your bank angle [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

bullets: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 ft; 1,000 fpm, 100 ft.
To cruise: smoothly lower the nose to the level attitude for cruise. Keep climb power while the airplane speeds up, then reduce to cruise power a bit before reaching cruise speed.
To stay at climb speed: lower the nose to the level attitude for that speed and reduce power at the same time.
Trim and go back to the straight-and-level cross-check.

body.p: Tolerances from ACS PA.VIII.B.S3. You must also enter the climb on an assigned heading (S1) and climb at constant airspeed to set altitudes, straight and in turns (S2). Climb speed and power come from your POH.

check.q: You're climbing at 700 fpm. When do you start leveling off?
check.a: About 70 ft before the target: 10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

body.p: Not speeding up the cross-check during speed, power or attitude changes is a common error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Watch for fixation, omission and emphasis, the same scan errors as in level flight [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Small, smooth pressures; check the result before adding more [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Chasing the airspeed to set the climb attitude
Set the attitude first, then fine-tune with airspeed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Not holding the new pitch as speed drops
Trim off pressures so you can tell your inputs from the airplane's [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Right rudder; don't fixate on the nose [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Cross-check it against the other pitch instruments [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not using the climb rate to set the level-off lead
Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Too much forward pressure at level-off
Lower the nose smoothly; it causes altitude loss or low G [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Slow cross-check as level flight returns
Keep scanning fast until fully established in level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]

callout.text: Small pitch changes are easy to control, stop and correct. Large ones aren't [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

check.q: Why trim during the climb entry?
check.a: Without trim you can't tell whether pressure changes come from the airplane or from your own hands [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

chunks.title: Risk: illusions, loss of control and getting help

body.p: Climbs bring their own illusions [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]:

head: Illusion
What you feel
Danger
rows: A slowly entered, coordinated turn feels like a climb
You misjudge your attitude unless you trust the instruments
An abrupt climb-to-level change feels like tumbling backward
You push abruptly nose-low, which makes it worse
You push into a nose-low or dive attitude

body.p: From [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]] and [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] (somatogravic from [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]). Smooth level-offs and trust in the instruments are the defense.

If a VFR pilot must climb in IMC, the AFH advice is to raise the nose no more than one bar width and add power, accepting whatever airspeed results. If the climb rate is too low, add power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch of manifold pressure [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Untrained pilots should avoid climbing turns if at all possible [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

callout.text: VFR pilots who haven't trained on instruments, or whose skills have faded, lose control in about 10 minutes on instruments alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Skills fade fast without practice [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

body.p: Get help early. You're in an urgency condition as soon as you're doubtful about weather, position or fuel [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. A non-instrument-rated pilot who can't stay VFR should tell ATC, say there's no instrument rating, and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. If ATC's urgency rushes you, ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

Fatigue degrades attention and narrows your focus to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]; heavy, ongoing stress makes performance fall off quickly [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. If you can't climb safely, a precautionary landing is less hazardous than waiting for a forced one [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: What can an abrupt level-off from a climb make you feel?
check.a: That you are tumbling backward (inversion illusion), which may lead you to push abruptly nose-low [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

body.p: In a climb the nose blocks your view ahead. VFR pilots adjust the pitch attitude in a climb to see better over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Under the hood you can't, so the safety pilot has to.

bullets: Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot with at least a private certificate for the airplane in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]].
The safety pilot needs good vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer to help [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].
Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during hood work; they must keep up the scan for traffic [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

callout.text: Brief before every hood session: who looks outside, how they'll call traffic, and the words for "take the controls".

check.q: Who is responsible for seeing traffic during a hood climb?
check.a: The safety pilot, who must have adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]] and keep scanning [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

f2.caption: Figure 7-26. Stabilized climb at constant airspeed.
f2.alt: Six-pack panel in a steady climb: airspeed indicator labeled primary pitch, heading indicator primary bank, attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank, VSI supporting pitch, turn coordinator supporting bank.

f3.caption: Figure 7-29. Level off at cruising speed.
f3.alt: Six-pack panel at level-off: altimeter labeled primary pitch, airspeed indicator primary power as airspeed approaches desired value, heading indicator primary bank, attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank.

f4.caption: Figure 6-20. Power and attitude equal performance.
f4.alt: Side view of a 5-minute climb: a light airplane climbs gently to about 2,500 ft over 7 and a half miles while a jet with the same attitude indicator picture climbs to 10,000 ft over 25 miles, with each airplane's airspeed and VSI shown.

f5.alt: Glass-cockpit primary flight display: small inset shows level flight at 5,000 ft; main display shows the yellow chevron raised, power increased to 25 inches and 2500 rpm, VSI showing 500 fpm, with labels for primary power, primary pitch and primary bank.

scenario.title: Climbing over the ridge in haze
scenario.setup: You are a private pilot with a passenger, headed home after a tiring day. Haze thickens as the terrain rises, and you lose the horizon. You need more altitude to clear a ridge ahead. Approach control has you on flight following and gives you a climb and a left turn at the same time, in a hurry.

questions.q: How should you make this climb?
questions.a: Wings level, raise the nose no more than one bar width, add power, and accept whatever airspeed results [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Expect the left-turning tendency and correct for it [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

questions.q: ATC wants a climbing turn now. What do you do?
questions.a: An untrained pilot should avoid combined maneuvers if possible [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]. Ask the controller to slow down, then turn and climb separately, with no more than 10° of bank [[24:370|AFH 18-21]] [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].
Yes. Say you can't stay VFR and have no instrument rating, and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Doubt about the weather was already an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

questions.q: The airspeed starts to creep up while the nose is still up. What do you check?
questions.a: Cross-check the attitude indicator, VSI, altimeter and power before acting. A blocked pitot tube and drain make the airspeed rise in a climb [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]; don't pull up to "fix" it.

questions.q: Over the ridge you level off quickly and feel like you're tumbling backward. What's happening?
questions.a: The inversion illusion from an abrupt climb-to-level change [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. Trust the attitude indicator and don't push the nose down.

You do. See-and-avoid stays with each pilot whenever weather permits, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. ATC traffic calls help but are given on a workload-permitting basis [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]], and your view ahead in a climb is poor [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Keep flying by the instruments, ask your passenger to help look, and listen for traffic calls.

questions.q: How did the tiring day matter?
questions.a: Fatigue degrades attention and coordination [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]], which is when fixation and omission set in [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Go from level flight to climb attitude and climb power on an assigned heading, with a proper cross-check and coordinated controls.
skills.practice: Practice entries from cruise and from climb speed, saying "pitch, power, right rudder, trim" aloud [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

skills.do: Climb at constant airspeed to assigned altitudes, straight ahead and in turns.
skills.practice: Have your CFI assign climbs with and without turns. Use standard-rate or shallower banks and speed up your scan [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

skills.do: Level off at the assigned altitude and hold altitude ±200 ft, heading ±20° and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.B.S3).
skills.practice: Call the lead point aloud: 10 percent of the VSI [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Keep the scan fast until level and trimmed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

quiz.q: Once stable in a constant-airspeed climb, which instrument is primary for pitch?
quiz.why: Once the climb stabilizes, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: You're climbing at 500 fpm. How far before your altitude do you start the level-off?
quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: Entering a climb from climb speed, you add power after raising the nose. What happens?
quiz.why: Power added after the pitch change shows a drop in airspeed from the extra drag [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

quiz.q: In a climb with high power, which way does the airplane tend to yaw, and what corrects it?
quiz.why: P-factor and torque roll and yaw the airplane left; use right rudder and aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

quiz.q: Your climb airspeed is 5 knots low. What's the right correction?
quiz.why: If the airspeed is low or high, make a small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: Leveling off to cruise speed, when do you reduce power?
quiz.why: Keep climb power to accelerate, then reduce to cruise power as airspeed approaches cruise [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: The static port blocks during a climb. What will the airspeed indicator show as you keep climbing?
quiz.why: Above the blockage altitude, trapped static pressure makes airspeed read lower than actual [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

quiz.q: An abrupt change from climb to level flight can cause which illusion?
quiz.why: It can feel like tumbling backward: the inversion illusion [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

takeaways: Climb power stays fixed; pitch holds the airspeed.
Entry: attitude first, then power, right rudder, trim. Once stable, airspeed is primary for pitch.
Climbing turns: straight-climb technique plus turn technique, shallow banks, faster scan.
Level off with a lead of 10 percent of the vertical speed; keep climb power until near cruise speed.
Smooth level-offs prevent the inversion illusion. Trust the instruments.
Under the hood, the safety pilot owns the outside scan.
cfi_notes: Most students overcontrol pitch on entry. Have them make the attitude change, then wait and look before adding more [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Point out that the attitude indicator sets pitch on entry, but the airspeed indicator takes over as primary once stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
In the airplane, have the student find the climb attitude picture for Vy and the pitch for cruise level-off; write them on a kneeboard.
Students on glass panels: show Figure 7-63 and the trend vector; the primary/supporting logic is the same.
Teach climbing turns only after straight climbs are solid; check for a slip that kills the climb rate [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Examiners often assign a climbing turn to a heading and altitude; watch for the student fixating on heading and losing airspeed.
gaps: Climb airspeed, climb power and the climb pitch attitude are airplane-specific; use the POH. The IFH examples use a sample retractable airplane.
The sources give no specific level-off lead for climbing turns or for rolling out and leveling at the same time; use the 10 percent and half-bank leads separately.
Emergency off-airport landings are covered only generically (AFH 18-1).

activities.title: Who's in charge right now?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Airspeed indicator in a steady constant-airspeed climb
VSI once a constant-rate climb has settled
Altimeter as you level off to cruise
Heading indicator in a straight climb
Heading indicator as you level off to cruise
Tachometer or manifold pressure in a steady constant-airspeed climb
Airspeed indicator once a constant-rate climb has settled
Airspeed indicator as the speed nears cruise at level-off

activities.title: True or false: can you trust it in a climb?

cards.s: A big, abrupt pitch change can make the VSI point the wrong way for a moment.
cards.why: Yes. A large, abrupt pitch change gives erratic needle movement and even a reverse indication [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

cards.s: The airspeed indicator has a large built-in lag, so ignore it during a climb entry.
cards.why: No. The instrument itself has no real lag. The delay you see is the airplane taking time to slow down or speed up [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

cards.s: If the static port blocks during a climb, the VSI keeps showing your climb rate.
cards.why: No. A blocked static system makes the VSI show zero all the time, and the altimeter freezes [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

cards.s: With the pitot tube and its drain hole both blocked, the airspeed reads higher as you climb.
cards.why: Yes. The trapped pitot pressure stays the same while outside pressure drops, so the indicator shows more speed [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

cards.s: The magnetic compass gives steady, reliable readings while you climb.
cards.why: No. Climbing, power changes and speed changes all affect the compass [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].

cards.s: During a rapid speed-up, the attitude indicator may show a slight nose-up.
cards.why: Yes. It can show slightly nose-up in rapid acceleration and nose-down in rapid deceleration [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

activities.title: Climb from cruise, then level off
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Raise the miniature airplane to the climb attitude with light back pressure
Add climb power as the airspeed nears climb speed
Once stable, hold the airspeed with small pitch corrections
Start the level-off 10 percent of the vertical speed before the altitude
Lower the nose smoothly to level, keeping climb power
Reduce to cruise power as the airspeed nears cruise
Trim and go back to the straight-and-level cross-check

activities.title: What should you do?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the best response.

pairs.r: Nose up no more than one bar width, add power
Add power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch
Ask the controller to slow down

pairs.l: Can't stay VFR, no instrument rating
pairs.r: Tell ATC you have no instrument rating and declare distress
You're already in an urgency condition: ask for help now
Trust the attitude indicator; don't push the nose down

final_quiz.q: You hold the same airspeed in a climb as in cruise. Why does the climb need more power?
options: The wing must make extra lift, which adds induced drag
The air gets denser as you climb, which adds drag
Parasite drag rises because the airplane flies faster
Weight increases when the nose is pointed up
final_quiz.why: Climbing takes extra lift, and extra lift makes extra induced drag. That's why a climb needs more power than level flight [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Weight stays the same.

final_quiz.q: During a long climb in an airplane with a normally aspirated engine, why do you keep nudging the throttle forward?
options: To keep the airspeed rising all the way up
Because P-factor gets weaker as you climb
Because the engine loses power in thinner air, so you hold climb power
To cool the engine with more airflow
final_quiz.why: Air density drops as you climb, so a normally aspirated engine makes less power. Keep advancing the throttle to hold the climb power setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying a constant-rate climb at 500 fpm. The VSI is right on 500, but the airspeed is 5 knots slow. What is the correction?
options: Lower the nose until the airspeed is back, and leave the power alone
Raise the nose slightly to hold the climb
Add power, and lower the nose slightly to keep 500 fpm
final_quiz.why: In a constant-rate climb, airspeed is controlled with power. If the vertical speed is right but the airspeed is low, add power and lower the nose slightly to hold the vertical speed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: You have started lowering the nose to level off at cruise speed. Which instrument is now primary for pitch?
final_quiz.why: At the level-off to cruise, the altimeter is primary for pitch. The airspeed indicator becomes primary for power as the speed nears cruise [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: You're climbing at a steady attitude and power when the airspeed slowly rises from 80 to 95 knots. You suspect the pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked. If you raise the nose to get 80 knots back, what happens?
options: Your real airspeed rises to match the indicator
The indicator drops back to 80 and all is well
Nothing changes, since the pitot system is sealed
Your real airspeed drops, and the indicator keeps rising as you climb
final_quiz.why: With the pitot tube and drain hole blocked, the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter and shows more speed as you climb [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. With power fixed, raising the nose slows the airplane [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Cross-check attitude and power instead.

final_quiz.q: You are climbing at 800 fpm to an assigned 6,500 feet. At what altimeter reading should you start the level-off?
final_quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed. 10 percent of 800 fpm is 80 feet, and 6,500 minus 80 is 6,420 feet [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: ATC asks you to level at 4,000 feet, and you want to stay at your climb airspeed. How do you level off?
options: Lower the nose to the level attitude for that speed and reduce power at the same time
Lower the nose and keep climb power until the airspeed builds
Reduce power first, then lower the nose a few seconds later
Keep the climb attitude and reduce power until the VSI reads zero
final_quiz.why: To level off at climb airspeed, lower the nose to the level attitude for that speed and reduce power at the same time. Done together, the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Keeping climb power is the method for leveling off at cruise speed.

final_quiz.q: In a straight climb, you roll into a 20° bank and keep the same climb power. Compared with the straight climb, what should you expect?
options: The same climb rate, since the power didn't change
A slightly shallower climb, and you need a bit more back pressure
A steeper climb, because the bank adds lift
Less back pressure is needed to hold the pitch
final_quiz.why: Some lift goes to turning, so the airplane climbs at a slightly shallower angle and needs extra back pressure. Steep banks cut the climb a lot [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: You will make a standard-rate climbing turn at 80 knots true airspeed. About how much bank do you need?
final_quiz.why: Use about 15 percent of true airspeed: divide by 10 and add half the result. 80 ÷ 10 = 8, plus 4 = 12° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

final_quiz.q: Under the hood, you climb holding firm back pressure on the yoke. You can't tell whether pitch changes come from the airplane or from your own hands. What common error is this?
final_quiz.why: Failure to trim off pressures is a common error. Unless the airplane is trimmed, it's hard to tell whether pressure changes come from the airplane or from you [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

final_quiz.q: A VFR pilot with no instrument training loses the horizon in haze and must climb to clear terrain. What technique does the AFH recommend?
options: Pitch for Vy and hold that exact airspeed
Make a climbing turn toward where the weather looked better
Raise the nose two or three bar widths and use full power
Raise the nose no more than one bar width, add power, and accept the airspeed you get
final_quiz.why: Raise the miniature airplane no more than one bar width and add power. Don't try for a set climb speed; accept whatever speed results [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. An untrained pilot should avoid climbing turns if at all possible [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: You level off abruptly from a climb and feel like you're tumbling backward. What is the danger if you act on that feeling?
options: You may roll into a steep bank
You may push the nose down abruptly, which makes the feeling worse
You may pull up into a stall
There is no danger, because the feeling is accurate
final_quiz.why: This is the inversion illusion. The pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude, which can make the illusion stronger [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. Trust the attitude indicator.

final_quiz.q: You plan to practice hood climbs with a friend as safety pilot. What must your friend have?
options: At least a private pilot certificate for the airplane's category and class, and a good view forward and to each side
A flight instructor certificate, in every case
Nothing special, as long as the friend sits up front and can see outside
final_quiz.why: The safety pilot in the other control seat must hold at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and have adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer to help [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].
